h: The politics of distraction: Gyanesh Kumar is being shielded
dek: According to Ravish Kumar, the 'regime change' issue is an attempt to turn eyes away from the real question, vote theft.
body: No straight answer to the allegations about SIR, the special intensive revision of electoral rolls, and vote theft has come till today. The writer reminds us that after many days of silence these allegations were tied to infiltration, without any solid ground being given for it. The home minister said the opposition was opposing SIR in order to protect infiltrators. The question is simple: in this process running since June last year, how many people were found to be infiltrators, and why is that figure not given.

The example of the Assam NRC was placed before people. That process cost more than 1,500 crore rupees, and lakhs of Hindus too reached the list of doubtful citizens. But in the first election held after the NRC, even its name stopped being mentioned. Now the same fear is being sold again under the name of SIR.

When attention did not move away from vote theft, efforts began to remove Jantar Mantar and to shut down the capital. The whole debate came round to the right to protest. When Gyanesh Kumar's question did not go away from there either, the issue of 'regime change' was pushed forward. According to the writer, this is the same old trick: instead of the real question, raise some other dispute even bigger than it.

In the meantime the commission is busy adding names. The writer asks what happened to the 27 lakh people whose names were cut. In Bihar and Bengal it was unlawful to cut names and stop people from voting, and this work happened before the eyes of the Supreme Court and the commission. If names are being added now out of fear of a crowd, they could have been added earlier too. It is because it cannot answer that the commission is silent, and to escape the public's question the stage of 'regime change' has been decorated.
nazar: Asking questions is not a crime in a democracy. When power, instead of giving an answer, makes the questioner the issue, it becomes clear that power does not have the answer.
Vote theft is not a political slogan, it is a question about trust in the election process. Until there is a public account of every name removed, doubt about election results will remain.
sawal: Why a new issue in place of an answer?
ref: Regime change
A demand to change the government. Here it has been used to turn attention away from the real question.
NRC
The National Register of Citizens in Assam, in which the citizenship of lakhs of people was declared doubtful.
ank: No account even after the names were cut

h: The power of the street: Congress is learning the language of protest again
dek: Anant Gupta writes that the young people of Jantar Mantar did what the party could not do in decades.
body: There is a new briskness in the steps of Congress leaders these days. Talking to several people in the party, it seems they see power as very close. One MP told the writer that chief election commissioner Gyanesh Kumar has given a face to the 'vote theft' allegations, one that an ordinary person can see and understand. That is why the party made the direct demand for his resignation its platform.

This change is surprising, because till a few months ago the party's own people used to explain that this way of protesting, and this time, were not right. At a meeting of the opposition alliance in June, Rahul Gandhi had questioned the CJP's demand against the then education minister. According to the writer, he called it 'low-hanging fruit', meaning an issue that is easy to pluck.

Then what changed inside the party. An official told the writer that in July the young man who handled their social media would say every evening that he was going home and go straight to Jantar Mantar, and stay there till three or four in the morning. This same generation did, in a few days, what big leaders could not do in decades. The official admitted that the leaders do not have that voice, because they live in fear.

Now the party is trying to keep this energy of the street alive. In July Rahul Gandhi and MPs had suddenly marched to the prime minister's residence, and after that many protests took place in Delhi. The party believes that the road to 2029 will go through the street alone. The writer also reminds us that the roots of the Congress lie in the movement itself, but there is also the question whether this enthusiasm will last or is only an attempt to make the most of the anger of the moment.
nazar: When the anger of the street becomes a party's agenda, its speed also starts to fall. The mood that the young people built does not belong to any one party.
The real test is whether the Congress only raises demands, or also speaks about its own mistakes and the weakness of its organisation.
sawal: How long will the party be able to speak the language of protest?
ref: CJP
Cockroach Janata Party, a movement of young people that forced the education minister to resign.
INDIA bloc
The election alliance of opposition parties, in which the Congress is the largest party.

h: The rule of fear: a government that has begun to fear slogans
dek: Apoorvanand writes that putting the whole force of the state against young people's slogans is proof of the government's weakness.
body: If the whole state stands up with all its force against someone, the first question that arises is who exactly is afraid. According to the writer, the one who is afraid is the one who steps out with sticks and guns to silence those raising slogans. Power has lost its sleep, opponents seem visible on every side, and because of this the police of every state are going round lane after lane.

Delhi Police, Bengal Police, the police of Gujarat and Madhya Pradesh, all are busy with one task: finding out whether some young person is going to the Jantar Mantar protest. The writer calls this not the protection of democracy but the politics of its fear. A government that trusts its own ability to put its case before the people is not afraid of peaceful protest.

The writer also reminds us that the right to protest is written in the Constitution, and the duty of upholding it does not rest on protesters alone. It rests also on those officers and security personnel who are given orders to shut the mouths of movement activists. What their conscience and their judgement say is a question the writer deliberately places before everyone.

So much fear of sloganeering that a large part of the capital is turned into a cantonment does not show the strength of power. In the writer's eyes it is a declaration that the government is in no position to answer its own citizens' questions. When arguments run out, then sticks and barricades come forward.
nazar: In a country where young people take to the street to say what they have in mind, and the government prepares only to stop them, democracy there becomes a thing on paper. Tolerating protest is also part of governing.
For the ordinary citizen the most important question is this: can I state my anger without fear? If the answer is no, then all the other rights are also incomplete.
sawal: What is there to fear in slogans?
ref: Jantar Mantar
An old designated site for protest in Delhi, from where a voice reaches the government.
Democratic legitimacy
The ground of power that comes from being chosen by the people, and stays alive by tolerating protest.

h: Jantar Mantar was ours: remembering a movement
dek: Asad Ashraf recalls how this square used to turn classroom, bookish debate into politics on the ground.
body: The writer's first meeting with Jantar Mantar came when he was a student at Jamia Millia Islamia and AISA's general secretary there. He was around twenty-one or twenty-two, had the confidence that the world could be changed by the force of certainty, and had also come to understand that nothing changes without a fight. In those days Jantar Mantar was like a second campus for him.

The piece reminds us that in the decades after independence the place of protest used to be the Boat Club lawn, right next to Parliament. In 1988 a gathering of lakhs of farmers under the leadership of Mahendra Singh Tikait took place at that very spot. In 1993 the Boat Club was banned, and then Jantar Mantar became the main protest site. It was close enough to Parliament for the voice to be heard, but the road was narrow enough for the government to keep it under control.

The standing of this place has never been settled. In 2017 the National Green Tribunal ordered that protests be stopped here, citing noise and garbage, but in 2018 the Supreme Court struck down the blanket ban on peaceful protest. Now in 2026 the Delhi Police has removed it from the list of designated protest sites and named alternatives such as Ramlila Maidan, Burari and CBD ground.

For the writer this is not simply a matter of a place being changed. At Jamia there used to be debates on Marx, imperialism and caste, but at Jantar Mantar those same things appeared in the form of people whose homes had been demolished, who had not been paid their wages, farmers sunk in debt and women who had been asking for pensions for years. Their lives became the proof of the bookish debate. That is why the site moving far away also means the voice will be gone before it reaches power.
nazar: The place of protest is also part of democracy. A protest pushed to a ground far from Parliament does not fall silent, but its voice becomes hard to hear.
Fixing a place in a city like Delhi is not only a traffic decision, it is a decision about whose voice will be heard from how far away.
sawal: To which corner of the city will the voice be pushed?
ref: Boat Club
An old protest site in Delhi near Parliament, from where protest moved to Jantar Mantar after a ban in the 1990s.
Ramlila Maidan
A large open ground in Delhi, now named as an alternative for protest.

h: Neha Bora: a new strategic link in the movement
dek: An analysis in Samkaleen Janmat says her rise is not the result of a viral moment but of long organising.
body: There is an easy way to understand anyone's public rise: place them on a level with some great historical hero. The article says this ease should be avoided, because it leaves out an examination of that person's hard work, ideological preparation and organisational experience. Neha Bora's rise should be seen on the same test.

Neha is a research scholar in theatre and performance studies at Jawaharlal Nehru University and the national president of the All India Students' Association. Her political upbringing came from theatre at Delhi University, feminist thought and student politics. According to the writer, this background shows that her personality is not the magic of some one reel or speech.

The movement at Jantar Mantar against irregularities in examinations gave her countrywide recognition for the first time. The early face of that movement was the CJP and Sonam Wangchuk, but AISA workers also pitched tents and began a hunger strike. When everyone else's eyes were on Wangchuk, AISA's fast stayed firm on its demands. Neha fasted for twenty-three days in June and July, lost eight kilos and had to be admitted to hospital, and even then she did not move from the demands.

The article's argument is that speaking before a crowd, and staying put with your colleagues even when support falls, are two different things. The importance of a hunger strike is not in its physical suffering but in the moral question it places before public life. The writer also accepts that no movement's victory belongs to one person alone, but it is also not right to make the role of someone who works continuously small by naming only the organisation.
nazar: Because of her association with a left-wing student organisation, Neha was long seen through one fixed slot. The article says a person's credibility should be decided by her demands and her work, not by her ideology.
When a woman's leadership becomes visible in a movement, there are also more questions about it. This article is an attempt to break that same prejudice.
sawal: Is leadership made by a single moment, or by years of work?
ref: AISA
All India Students' Association, a left-wing student organisation.
Hunger strike
A way of protesting by giving up food when a demand is not met, in which a health risk has to be taken.

h: Barricades and detention: a smell like the Emergency
dek: Mohit M. Rao reports that an elderly man from Bihar could not reach Jantar Mantar even after a two-day journey.
body: Shivmuni Singh, 74, who came from Bihar's Buxar district, asked how any democratic government could do this. He had travelled for two days, spent the night at a railway station on the outskirts of Delhi and reached here, but could not go past the barricade put up in the middle of the city. Jantar Mantar was still two and a half kilometres away and more than two hundred policemen were posted at that barricade.

The article reports that on 10 October the Cockroach Janata Party announced a protest in Delhi against chief election commissioner Gyanesh Kumar. The allegation is that unlawful methods were used in the special intensive revision of voter rolls, because of which minority and opposition voters were targeted. According to the writer, 13 crore names have already been removed in this process, and the opposition in several states says this helped the BJP win elections.

Shivmuni Singh had first seen a video of CJP founder Abhijeet Dipke during the students' movement in July. His father had gone to jail in the freedom struggle, so speaking on the country's issues came naturally to him. He was among the few people who could get past layer after layer of barricades to reach the administrative area of the capital.

The article details the strictness of the Delhi Police, the condition of the people on hunger strike and the detentions. The writer says the situation is beginning to be compared with the Emergency of 1975, when newspapers were censored and opponents were put in jail without trial. Even today a large number of people have been taken into custody, but the government calls it only a matter of law and order.
nazar: When an elderly man has to cross two and a half kilometres of barricades just to ask his elected government one question, the meaning of democracy changes.
The comparison with the Emergency should be made carefully, not in haste, but if censorship, detention and a ban on protest appear together, it becomes a worry.
sawal: What is the price of asking a question in a democracy?
ref: Emergency
The Emergency imposed between 1975 and 1977, in which civil rights and the freedom of the press were curtailed.
Barricade
A fence put up to block a road so that protesters cannot move forward.

h: Neha means love: gentleness even in anger
dek: Amina writes that Neha Bora's voice made a place of its own for women in the movement.
body: In the first wave of July, Neha Bora was far from the stage. Then she was only a student on hunger strike, whose fast was proof of young people's anger. According to the writer, her voice reached people slowly, the way a smouldering fire is seen late. In her speech there was anger, and also that warmth which makes even the most stubborn listener bend.

A large part of the article is about the difference that a woman's voice makes. The writer says men have learnt more the manner of inflaming a crowd, but Neha's voice works not through noise but through a quiet awakening. People may not agree after hearing her speeches, but they become ready to listen.

During the movement she was taken into custody from Jantar Mantar. She was part of the demand, along with the INDIA bloc, for SIR, the special intensive revision of electoral rolls, to be withdrawn. The writer recalls that photograph in which she sits in red clothes with her head resting on her hand, a smile on her face and small plants growing around her. Even in the bus, when someone outside asked for a bottle of water, it was she who reached forward and gave it.

The writer believes that the very meaning of Neha's name is love, and perhaps that is the truest identity of her political personality. In a society where even a woman's anger is heard only on condition that it stays within the bounds of decorum, a woman standing in an open ground and speaking in her own voice is a statement in itself.
nazar: When the face of a movement is a woman, the demands change too. It is not only electoral reform, the right of a woman to stand on the street also comes into the debate.
It is easy to take Neha's popularity as the magic of one person alone, but behind her are long strikes, organisation and the everyday struggle of students.
sawal: How much room does a woman's anger get?
ref: AISA
All India Students' Association, the left-wing student organisation whose national president Neha Bora is.
Hunger strike
A way of protesting by giving up food for an indefinite period when a demand is not met.

h: Europe's young people on the street: the question of rent and livelihood
dek: From France to Spain and Italy, prices, housing and the state of schools have brought young people out on the street.
body: In Europe the streets this autumn are full of anger. Rising fuel prices, the poor state of schools, shrinking public services and a housing crisis, all four together are making a season in which protest keeps spreading. France, Italy and Albania have seen violence, arrests and looting, while in Spain and Portugal people have pitched tents and are sitting in protest against rents.

Quoting the Spanish sociologist Maria Silvestre, the article says young people are disillusioned with the social model and no longer have a sense of control. When several conditions worsen together, one spark brings the whole discontent onto the street. This is not only a crisis of politics, it is a crisis of livelihood.

In France high school students have been blockading schools and protesting for three weeks. They say schools in low-income areas have both fewer teachers and fewer facilities. Trade unions joined them too, and the demands spread to prices and public services. Despite peaceful marches, 2,400 people were arrested over the weekend, shops were looted in Paris, Marseille, Lyon and Bordeaux, and a nineteenth-century city hall in Limoges burnt to ashes.

In the Spanish capital, tarpaulin tents have stood at Puerta del Sol for several weeks. This protest began after an 87-year-old woman was evicted from her home, and she died in hospital. The government approved rent control measures, but they did not pass for want of support in parliament and elections had to be announced for November. In Spain the minimum wage is 1,221 euros, while the average rent for an eighty square metre home is around 1,130 euros. In Italy too prices have risen to 4.2 per cent and two days of violence in Milan led to 271 arrests.
nazar: This anger in Europe is not imported. When rent eats up wages and no teachers are left in schools, the language of politics changes. Right-wing parties are trying to turn this same anger towards infiltration and race.
The lesson for India is clear: young people's discontent needs answers on jobs, rent and public services, not only speeches.
sawal: If rent eats up the wages, where will the anger go?
ref: Puerta del Sol
The central square of Madrid, where people have pitched tents and are living in protest against rents.
Rent control
Steps by which a government fixes a limit on rent, so that tenants get relief.

h: Politics in the Ramlila: is the BJP's grip loosening?
dek: Several mandals now want to keep politicians away from the Dussehra stage, and this change has not come by itself.
body: For three decades the BJP has built a large part of its political identity in the name of Ram. After the temple was built in Ayodhya, the claim looked even more settled that Ram belonged politically to it alone. This Dussehra several Ramlila mandals are saying that religion and politics should be kept apart. Among them are mandals whose office bearers or trustees include people from the BJP.

Arjun Kumar, associated with Delhi's Lav Kush Ramlila and the Shri Ramlila Mahasangh, says many devotees do not agree with the BJP's politics, and earlier they felt they were drifting away. According to him, religion should not discriminate in this way, so the change was made. The article only asks why this change now, when for years this same stage was used politically.

Questions have begun to be raised about the temple built in Ayodhya itself, and there is a debate over its construction, its management and the money donated. Hanumangarhi's mahant Raju Das accepts that the mandals feel the presence of politicians on the stage has now become awkward. The writer calls this only speculation, but also says that because of the temple's political importance such questions are the most painful for the BJP.

A similar signal comes from Kutch in Gujarat. Sameer Garg, head of a large mandal in Gandhidham, says there is a big gap between the claim of development and conditions on the ground. Questions are being raised about malnutrition, unemployment and the plight of farmers, and there is also talk of small traders being hurt by GST and demonetisation. This time his mandal decided not to put any politician's picture on its banners, because while asking for donations the workers got to hear the anger directly.
nazar: Keeping politicians off the Ramlila stage is in itself a big political event. It means the pairing of temple and electoral gain no longer looks right to every devotee.
This question is also necessary: is this a victory of principle or of compulsion? If the anger is only about claims of development, then it is a warning for any party.
sawal: When does the pairing of religion and elections break?
ref: Ramlila mandal
Local committees that stage the Ram story at Dussehra, and whose social and political influence is large.
Creamy layer
The debate about keeping a separate group, within reservation, of those whose economic condition has already improved.
photo_note: Sita and Luv in a Kalighat painting, representative image

h: Whose Hindi is it: a different date that emerges from books
dek: Tyler Williams's book shows that Hindi was never one clean language decided from the top.
body: Tyler Williams's book, If All the World Were Paper, writes the physical date of Hindi's writing. The book treats language not as a thing decided from above but as a thing made of paper, manuscripts and everyday use. The writer says there is a quietly placed argument in it, which turns upside down today's debates about purity in Hindi.

The book opens the world of old manuscripts, in which the Sharada, Devanagari and Gujarati scripts move together. Literature written in different forms such as pem-katha, gutka, pothi and vani shows that the language had no single home. In the writer's words, Williams deliberately moves towards a language and a literature built from the bottom up, a little untidy.

Today Hindi is often used as the language of power. A standard Hindi is imposed in schools, in names and in government papers, and this language also produces resistance across a large part of the country. The book challenges the notion that there was once one clean, uniform Hindi which was later spoilt.

According to the article, this history is not only an academic debate. When politics decides what real Hindi is, it also decides whose speech, whose writing and whose folk knowledge will be pushed to the margins. The strength of this book is that it shows language as an open space in which many voices have always lived.
nazar: If Hindi's variety is not treated as a weakness, school syllabi and translation can change too. To seat the authority of a language at the centre is to deny its oldest tradition.
In India language too carries the politics of caste, gender and region. To write the date of Hindi is to write the date of that politics.
sawal: Why does power take itself to be the owner of a language?
ref: Gutka
A small Devanagari booklet in which devotional poems or texts were collected.
Pem-katha
Stories of devotion and love, heard and read in different scripts and regions.
photo_note: A manuscript page written in Devanagari

h: Cuba's upper hand: bluster is loud, but bluster is what loses
dek: Mario Reinaldo Machado writes that despite a 60-year blockade this island has kept teaching the world to ask questions.
body: Cuba is once again in America's sights. The action in Venezuela earlier this year is being seen as the road to a similar attempt on this island. American officials are saying openly that they want Cuba free, and there are also reports of military activity around it. According to the writer, it is still not clear when and how an attack would come, but neighbourhood by neighbourhood a feeling is building that the end of the revolution is near.

The article sees Cuba as Eshu, the god of the Santeria tradition, who is the guardian of roads and a bridge between past and future, and whose mischievous tales hold a mirror to power. The writer says Cuba should be understood in this way: it questioned the shape the world is in, and at the same time made even the most powerful country look small.

There are many examples of this in the article. In 1960, when the big hotels of the city refused to let Cuban leaders stay there, they stayed in a small hotel in Harlem. After this the government built its reach into the poor countries of the world through doctors, engineers and technicians. About four lakh doctors were sent to 164 countries, and in Angola more than three lakh soldiers fought a war whose effect reached the end of South Africa's apartheid regime.

An American economic blockade has been in place for sixty years, described as the longest blockade in the world. The island also came through the crisis after the break-up of the Soviet Union, and in many difficult periods stayed ahead of America in figures such as literacy and child mortality. The writer believes that if this revolution ends, the world will also lose a voice that was once heard.
nazar: Cuba's name today is tied to economic hardship and political uniformity, and covering that part would also be wrong. But the article's question comes to rest in the very period when a big power is thinking of tossing it like a coin.
Change loaded from outside in the name of democracy and equality, where has it ever given a better result first? This question is necessary for the Global South.
sawal: Can a country be changed without asking its opinion?
ref: Eshu
In Cuba's Santeria tradition, the god of crossroads and roads, who stands for both mischief and awareness.
Operation Carlota
The name given to Cuba's military involvement in Angola, which changed the direction of the anti-apartheid struggle.

h: Rule of the Thai army: a democracy that had to be stopped every time
dek: Paul Chambers's analysis shows that since 1932 the Thai army does not leave the scene even after elections are won.
body: In Thailand, since the end of monarchical rule in 1932, the army has taken direct control of power 14 times. This figure by itself says that holding elections does not make a democracy. In his speech Chambers calls the army a force painted in the colours of the monarchy, meaning a power that cannot be understood apart from the institution of the throne.

After Black May in 1992 the country got a form of democracy in which elections kept happening, but decisions stayed in the hands of the traditional elite and the army. After Thaksin Shinawatra came to power in 2001 this balance broke, and in 2006 the army staged a coup again. After this, defence law and the internal security system were made stronger, so that in the posting of military officers the army's own practice became the norm.

The 2014 coup and military rule weakened democratic institutions. The 2017 constitution opened the way for nominated members in the upper house, and political parties remained under pressure. In 2019 the army-backed party helped keep a former coup leader as prime minister. In 2023 the leader of the party that came ahead in the election was kept out of power only because of this, which the writer calls the limit of the system.

The writer calls the present prime minister, Anutin Charnvirakul, not an agent of change but a guardian of the status quo. In the 2025 Thai-Cambodia border clash the army's image rose again and in a survey 62.5 per cent of people expressed trust in the army. The writer believes the government saves its own power by giving the army leeway in matters such as defence spending, border policy and reinstatement, and this same bargain keeps the system alive.
nazar: Thailand's example shows that democracy does not stay alive only on election day. The army, the monarchy and the design of the constitution decide how much the people's vote will do.
In South and Southeast Asia this question returns everywhere: will institutions be reformed, or only the game of votes?
sawal: Why is the road to power shut even after winning?
ref: Black May
The army's firing on pro-democracy protesters in Bangkok in May 1992, in which hundreds of people were killed.
Internal Security Act
A Thai law that gives ISOC wide powers of arrest, surveillance and security inside the country.

h: Tagore's wall: the parting of a heritage in Bangladesh
dek: After Rabindranath's picture was painted over in Dhaka, his own songs were sung, and the internet laughed.
body: On a Saturday afternoon some young people in Dhaka decided that Rabindranath Tagore should be wiped out. Among the Bangladeshi cultural faces painted on a newly built wall outside the Shilpakala Academy, they began to smear ink on his picture. The police came in between and four people were taken into custody. They were accused of conspiracy and of spreading religious hatred.

A young woman gave her reason: this was a protest against India's power. That is, Tagore is not the poet born in Bengal decades before Partition, but an Indian marker that should be removed from the wall. The writer calls this argument historically poor, but asks why the reaction was even more surprising than that.

After that people from the cultural organisation Udichi gathered below the wall. Someone was playing a harmonium, someone was singing, and all together they sang 'Ekla Chalo Re'. There was no stage, the wires lay on the ground. But the video that went on television got about 40 thousand reactions, of which nearly 95 per cent were laughter.

The writer says this laughter should not be taken as public opinion, but its measure cannot be ignored either. In Bangladesh Tagore has almost become a religion, with its own priests and fixed interpretations. In the time of the Hasina government he was given a place in official rituals, and as heritage came to be run on a political base, that same religion became a target of taunts. According to the writer, making the poet a national monument kills his restless, arguing voice.
nazar: The debate over cultural identity in Bangladesh did not begin with anti-India feeling; after the 2024 coup it took on a new colour. In both countries Tagore has again become a question.
To make a writer a symbol of the nation is not to honour him, it is to confine him. No one has a sole claim on Bengal's shared heritage.
sawal: Who wins by wiping the poet off a wall?
ref: Ekla Chalo Re
Tagore's Bengali song, which gives the courage to walk alone on the path of truth.
Udichi
A cultural organisation in Bangladesh that works for unity through music and theatre.
photo_note: A portrait of Rabindranath Tagore, in thought

h: 1,100 Muslim families made homeless in Assam in two days
dek: In Nagaon, Golaghat and Hojai, under an anti-encroachment drive, the homes of more than 1,100 families were demolished and more than ten mosques were pulled down.
body: In a two-day anti-encroachment drive in Assam more than 1,100 Muslim families were evicted, most of them Bengali-speaking Muslims. According to a Maqtoob Media report, the action took place in the Nagaon, Golaghat and Hojai districts. On the first day 547 families were displaced, of which 336 were from Nagaon, 152 from Hojai and 59 from Golaghat. On the second day the homes of more than 600 families were demolished in Lutumari Longjap reserved forest in Nagaon.

The administration says these families had encroached on forest land. The people displaced in Lutumari refuse to accept this claim. They say they were earlier labourers of the Forest Department and it was the government that settled them there. According to the report these families had been living on more than 300 hectares of land for decades. In June the All India Union of Forest Working People had demanded that the eviction be stopped.

The union's argument was that the people of these villages were settled under the Toungya system of the colonial period, so they cannot be treated as ordinary encroachers. The report quotes a local resident as saying that in 1974 the government settled 300 landless families by giving each of them four bighas of land, and that their ancestors were from a nearby town.

More than ten mosques were also pulled down in the drive, some of them more than fifty years old. The report also says that people who had lived there for decades had also taken the route to court against eviction. Action of this kind against Bengali-speaking Muslims has been going on in the state before this too.
nazar: In Assam eviction now looks like a campaign against one particular community. When people settled on forest land for decades, settled by the government itself, suddenly become encroachers, the question that arises is not of law but of the choices of power.
Under the Forest Rights Act, people should be protected from being displaced until their claim has been examined. Bulldozers moving even after a court has been approached hollows out that protection.
sawal: Why was the forest rights claim not examined before the eviction?
ref: Toungya system
A colonial-era arrangement in which labourers were settled on Forest Department land for temporary cultivation, and in return worked for the department.
Reserved forest
A forest area under government control, where human settlement and cultivation are barred by law.

h: Newspaper bureau chief beaten to death in Hapur
dek: After the death of Mohammad Naseem Ahmed, bureau chief of Dainik Janwani, in a dispute said to be over asking for a Diwali advertisement, the police have taken two people into custody for questioning.
body: There are reports of the beating to death of Mohammad Naseem Ahmed, bureau chief of the Hindi newspaper Dainik Janwani, in Uttar Pradesh's Hapur district. On Sunday afternoon in the Jarothi Road area he had gone with some people to a flour mill to ask for a Diwali advertisement for the newspaper. He was 60 years old and the incident is from the Hapur Dehat police station area.

According to a Maqtoob Media report, eyewitness Salauddin says that mill owner Ashok Kumar refused to give the advertisement and, as they were leaving, called him a fake journalist. After this a group of about seven or eight people beat up Ahmed and Salauddin.

According to the complaint of Dr Shahrukh at Hapur Dehat police station, his wife called to say that her father had been beaten mercilessly. On reaching the community health centre he spoke to Salauddin, Mustaqeem, Monika and Shahana. These people said they had gone with Ahmed to Ashok Kumar Gupta's mill to ask for an advertisement.

The complaint accuses Gupta, his son Kapil, Naresh Kumar and four or five unknown people of abuse and assault. When Ahmed objected to the abuse, the accused rained kicks and punches on him and struck his chest again and again. Superintendent of police Madhuban Kumar has confirmed the death and said that two people have been taken into custody for questioning. Further legal action will follow the result of the investigation.
nazar: Journalists running newspapers in small towns work under pressure from both advertisements and news. When asking for an advertisement puts a life at risk, the freedom of the press is no longer a matter of big cities and big newsrooms alone.
The investigation into the killing should clearly show the side of power, otherwise this case too will sink into a file.
sawal: How did a journalist who went to ask for an advertisement lose his life?
ref: Bureau chief
The journalist in charge of a newspaper in a particular area, who looks after both its news and its advertisements.
Community health centre
A government primary hospital in towns and villages, where the first, urgent treatment is available.

h: Declaring themselves dead, 37 people applied to have their names removed
dek: During SIR in Karnataka, 37 people filled Form 7 to have their own names removed from the voter list by calling themselves dead, and 334 pairs declared each other dead.
body: In Karnataka, during the special intensive revision of the voter list, at least 37 people applied to have their own names removed from the list by declaring themselves dead. The Wire Hindi gave this information quoting an analysis by The Hindu. The analysis also brought out that 334 pairs had declared each other dead.

In such a pair, one person filled Form 7 to remove the other's name and gave death as the reason, and then the person declared dead also filled the same form. The analysis of Election Commission data found that both people in every pair were listed in the voters' list of the same polling station. At least three forms were filled after the draft list was printed, which means those people's names were in the draft.

The report also points to the suspicion of a software error. In Byatarayanapura, the name of 25-year-old Sudha KN was found recorded both as the person filling the form and as the one whose name was to be removed. The booth level officer said the form asked for Srikanth's name to be removed and his wife had filled it, but in the list the name of Sudha appeared in place of Srikanth. The officer could not explain the reason for the error.

Earlier it had come out that details of 28,832 Form 7s in the state were not made public. Between 16 June and 28 August, 1,10,654 forms were filled, while 81,822 were recorded on the commission's portal. A district officer had alleged pressure to remove about three thousand names. It also came out that most of the forms demanded the removal of Muslim voters' names.
nazar: The biggest loss from a mess in the voter list falls on people who do not have the time and the means to file a complaint. Here most of the forms were against Muslim voters, which means the cutting of names was targeted in advance.
Whether it is a software error or intent, accountability should be fixed in both cases.
sawal: Who will investigate the mess in removing names?
ref: Form 7
The form for having someone's name removed from the voter list, or for filing an objection.
SIR
The special intensive revision of the voter list, in which names and eligibility are checked again.

h: Muslim influencer's garba events cancelled in Jaipur
dek: After warnings from Hindutva organisations, organisers withdrew two events of Javed Ali Khan, while the police denied knowing of any protest.
body: In Jaipur two proposed appearances of social media influencer Javed Ali Khan at Navratri garba events were cancelled. According to The Wire Hindi, the organisers said Hindutva organisations objected on the ground that Khan is not a Hindu and threatened vandalism if the events were not cancelled.

Molis Club owner Ravi Patel said on 18 October that the event was cancelled after objections from several organisations including the Vishva Hindu Parishad and the Bajrang Dal. He had received many calls and messages which carried warnings of vandalism. Khan was to attend the event as a guest with his family. Patel says the police too gave a similar warning later.

Khan's presence at a dandiya event at Vinaya Resort on 17 October was also cancelled. Khan, 31, said the organiser sent him an audio in which the Sanatan Suraksha Dal warned against inviting him. Khan returned the advance and said he did not want anyone to suffer because of him. Sanatan Suraksha Dal founder Ravi Gautam admitted giving the warning and said garba is tied to the worship of Hindu goddesses.

According to Gautam, people of the organisation are checking the identity of those coming to the pandals and putting tilak on their foreheads. Their team has so far visited 70 to 80 pandals. Police officer Shiv Dayal Meghwal said he had no information of any such protest. PUCL's Kavita Srivastava opposed this and asked the government to intervene.
nazar: Dragging a folk celebration like garba into the ambit of religious vetting is the clearest form of communalism. When organisers withdraw events out of fear, the state's job stops being only to keep law and order.
The shrinking of public stages for Muslim artists is a question about the public life of the whole community.
sawal: Who will decide who takes part in a festival?
ref: Sanatan Suraksha Dal
A Hindutva organisation formed in Jaipur six months ago, which claims to check people's identity in garba pandals.
PUCL
People's Union for Civil Liberties, an organisation that works for civil rights.

h: Dalit youth beaten in Ballia for praying at a temple
dek: In Sardaspur village, an FIR has been registered against two people on charges of beating and holding captive Nagina Ram, who lives in the compound of the Kali temple.
body: In Sardaspur village of Uttar Pradesh's Ballia district a case has come to light of a Dalit youth being beaten over praying at a temple and living there. The victim, Nagina Ram, lived in the compound of the village's Kali temple and prayed there every day. According to The Mooknayak's report, the incident is from the evening of Sunday, 18 October.

According to the complaint, two youths began to abuse him without provocation, cursed him over his caste and beat him. When villagers working in nearby fields heard the noise and ran to help, the accused locked Nagina Ram inside the temple compound and held him captive. According to the report, they then went to his house and threatened to kill him in front of his family.

The complaint was registered at Rasra police station late on Sunday night. Station house officer Sushil Kumar confirmed the incident and said that on Nagina Ram's complaint a named FIR has been registered against Vishal Singh and Ankit Singh. The case is registered under provisions of the Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita and the Scheduled Castes and Scheduled Tribes (Prevention of Atrocities) Act.

The police have said that a team is investigating the matter and collecting evidence. The station house officer told the victim's side that necessary legal action will be completed with full strictness and without pressure, and that the administration is keeping an eye on peace and law and order in the village. This case over the right to pray at the temple and to live there brings old complaints of caste discrimination to the front again.
nazar: Dalits got the right to enter temples from courts and the law, but the duty of enforcing it in villages rests with the police and the administration. A named FIR is the first step, not justice.
When the victim is living alone and the whole village stands in the middle, the administration's eye is his protection.
sawal: Why is the right to pray in a temple tied to caste?
ref: Scheduled Castes and Scheduled Tribes (Prevention of Atrocities) Act
A law that provides strict punishment for caste atrocities against Dalits and Adivasis.
Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita
The new criminal law, which replaced the Indian Penal Code in 2024.

h: Court extends custody of Saurav Das and Ranka by two days
dek: The special executive magistrate said the conduct of both does not show respect for the law and that the apprehension of a breach of peace is serious.
body: A special executive magistrate's court in Delhi on Monday, 19 October, extended the judicial custody of Cockroach Janata Party workers Saurav Das and Ashutosh Ranka by two days. Magistrate Ritu Raj said the conduct of both shows that they have no respect for the law in their minds and that the apprehension of a breach of peace is serious.

The court held that their statement that they would not do this again is not trustworthy, because they have done it before as well. The court said that by calling for protest in de-notified areas they acted habitually. The court found the investigating officer's application supported by material on record.

The court found both sureties of Ranka and Das ineligible. In one surety's bond, a difference was found between the photograph and the Aadhaar card, and his replies were not satisfactory. The second surety could not give basic information about Das, and neither surety could give an assurance of producing them in court. The court directed that new sureties be given and posted the matter for hearing on 21 October.

The police told the court that the two broke the condition of the bond given on 11 October and called people to gather at Jantar Mantar, which has been removed from the list of protest sites. The police also said that the two called people for protest on social media. The defence called the allegations false and demanded immediate release. Both were taken into custody on 13 October.
nazar: Fixing a place for protest is the administration's right, but it should be the same for everyone. Extending custody again and again in the name of a possible breach of peace turns into punishment, while guilt has yet to be proved.
If de-notifying Jantar Mantar itself becomes the way to stop dissent, where will protest happen in a democracy?
sawal: How justified is detention on the apprehension of a breach of peace?
ref: Special executive magistrate
An officer of the district administration who decides bail and bonds in cases involving the apprehension of a breach of peace.
De-notified protest site
A place that has been removed from the list of approved protest sites, such as Jantar Mantar.

h: Adivasi homes razed in Kosmi, forest rights claim still pending
dek: In Madhya Pradesh's Nasrullaganj, the Forest Development Corporation pulled down the huts of 12 Barela families and destroyed standing crops.
body: In Kosmi village of Nasrullaganj (now Bhairunda) in Madhya Pradesh, on the night of 11 October a team of the Forest Development Corporation arrived with four excavators and four tractors. The team pulled down the temporary huts of 12 families on the charge of occupying forest land. According to Down To Earth's report, all these families belong to the Barela Adivasi (indigenous) community.

In the drive standing crops of maize and pigeon pea were also destroyed and a well used for irrigation was filled with soil and stones. According to the report the families were also threatened with eviction. The village is in Singpur gram panchayat and lies among dense forests towards the Narmada valley, south of Bhopal. There are 145 houses and 998 Adivasi residents here.

A resident named Ikram Barela does not have a document of ownership of the land, but he has the government receipt that recognises his claim recorded under the Forest Rights Act. The claim was filed on 11 December 2025, the land was inspected on 18 July 2026 and the claim was sent to the district committee on 7 August. Till 15 October the decision was pending.

After the incident Union Agriculture Minister Shivraj Singh Chouhan raised a public voice against the action and sat on a dharna, a sit-in protest. In the collector's inquiry ordered by chief minister Mohan Yadav, nine people were described as encroachers and it was claimed that they had occupied 31.48 hectares of forest land by destroying 78,700 teak saplings. Section 4(5) of the Forest Rights Act gives protection from eviction until a claim is settled.
nazar: The forest rights law was made so that people living in the forests for generations would get rights instead of papers. When forest department land is handed to the corporation for large-scale plantation, those claims should be examined first.
For Adivasi families, home, crop and well going together is a question of livelihood, not of land alone.
sawal: Why did the bulldozer move while the claim was pending?
ref: Forest Rights Act
A 2006 law that recognises the land rights of Adivasis and forest dwellers living in forests.
Forest Development Corporation
A state government company that does commercial plantation and timber production on forest land.

h: Ultimatum to vacate mosque near PM's residence
dek: The imam of a mosque on Race Course Road, more than 100 years old, alleges that electricity and water were cut off and that he was told to vacate the place within six days.
body: In Delhi a mosque in the Race Course area, more than a hundred years old, faces the threat of demolition. The mosque's imam, Mohammad Haroon, alleges that he has been told to vacate the place within six days. The mosque is near Prime Minister Narendra Modi's residence.

According to Siyasat Daily's report, the imam said the mosque's electricity and water connections have been cut and worshippers have stopped coming out of fear of action. He says all the mosque's bills have been paid on time and there was no complaint of any kind.

The mosque is recorded under the Delhi Waqf Board, and the report says it has seating for 800 worshippers. The imam alleges that he asked the board to go to court, but there was no reply. He said that if the board does not go, he will go himself.

Aam Aadmi Party leader and former MLA Amanatullah Khan said the mosque was built before independence and is recorded in the notified heritage list of the New Delhi Municipal Council. All India Majlis-e-Ittehadul Muslimeen's Delhi president Shoaib Jamai said this mosque on Race Course Road is 125 years old, as recorded in a 1977 gazette notification. His question was that if an official comes and threatens to demolish a mosque within a week and walks away, how is the government being run.
nazar: In Delhi mosques and graveyards are under constant pressure. When a place of worship is emptied by cutting power and water and by handing out ultimatums, the question is not about one building but about the public life of minorities.
The silence of the Waqf Board and the action of the administration, the accountability of both should be fixed.
sawal: Whose land is the listed heritage mosque on?
ref: Waqf Board
The state board that looks after Muslim religious properties and places of worship.
Notified heritage list
The government's list in which historic buildings are recorded, and for which rules of conservation are made.

h: The rains changed, and so did the Bakarwal route
dek: Bakarwal herders of Rajouri are getting caught between changing weather and the high pastures, and trucks have now taken the place of migration on foot.
body: In the Kalakote block of Rajouri district, the flock of seventy goats and sheep of Javed Khatana moves restlessly on a dry slope. He says grass used to stay green longer, now everything changes quickly. Sometimes rain lasts till the end of spring, sometimes a sudden spell of heat dries everything up. This affects the animals' stomachs and their strength to bear disease.

In April 2026 the hill at Kalakote was unusually silent. The grass in the pastures below had run low, but in the high pastures of Kashmir and Ladakh grass fit for grazing had not yet grown. Shafi Mohammad says that if they leave early there is no fodder in the dok, and if they wait the pastures below are finished. In the winter of 2025-26 rainfall was sixty-five per cent below normal.

This uncertainty has changed the old route. Earlier Bakarwals went up on foot over a month, now most hire trucks. One round from Rajouri to Srinagar costs twenty-five to thirty thousand rupees, and the whole cycle fifty to sixty thousand. Those who walk are now looked on as backward. The journey is done in a day or two, but the animals do not get time to get used to the new cold and the grass.

The burden of change is not the same for everyone. Shakina Begum, eighty, says sitting long in a truck tires you more than walking. For younger women the route has become lighter, because the cooking work at the camps has reduced. But young people are taking up wage work in towns. The elder Farooq says that children used to learn every leaf, every hill and every spring of water along the way.
nazar: Herders are the first witnesses of climate change, but the cost of adapting comes out of their own pockets. Truck fare, costly fodder and medicine, all three together turn the blow of weather into an economic blow.
If pastoralism is to be kept alive, access to the high pastures, help with fares and animal health arrangements will have to become a public responsibility in the same way as it is for farming.
sawal: The weather has changed, so who will save the herder's route?
ref: Dok
The high pastures of Kashmir and Ladakh, where Bakarwals take their flocks in summer.
Bakarwal
A community that moves from place to place with livestock in the hill areas of Jammu and Kashmir.

h: Tenyidie comes alive through reels and memes
dek: In Kohima, teachers and young people are trying to bring the mother tongue of the Angami community back into everyday life through social media.
body: In a school in Kohima, Rohvilheu finds it awkward to speak her mother tongue Tenyidie; it sounds formal. Even joking with friends at school often does not happen in the mother tongue. Tenyidie is the language of the Angami community, which UNESCO has placed among vulnerable languages. According to the 2011 census it had more than one lakh twenty-one thousand speakers in Kohima, and the dialect of almost every village is different.

The language is taught till class twelve and there is a PhD in it too, yet young people keep it limited to the classroom and cultural events. Teacher Zhosahu started a group for learning Tenyidie on Facebook. The first video of a seminar by the Ura Academy was watched more than a thousand times. After that people began asking how to say hello, the words for relationships, proverbs and everyday words.

Teacher Kikruneinuo Zed B Liezietsu says the language has to be made an everyday need, not a museum piece. According to her, it is necessary to bring the language back to reels, to memes and to all the places where young people spend their time. She runs the Ura Academy's social media page and is getting young creators to make short skits, bilingual poems and remixes of folk songs.

There are hurdles on the way too. Because it is written in the Roman script, spelling does not stay uniform, and decorative fonts confuse learners. Money is short, so this work is mostly done for free, and Zhosahu accepts that he cannot post regularly. College student Nevinuo says young people are certainly moving away from the culture, but they were never told how to connect the language to life today.
nazar: Saving a language does not mean keeping it under lock. The language in which memes are made, songs are made and everyday talk happens is the one that reaches the next generation.

This work at present rests on the free time and unpaid labour of a few teachers. It is easy to treat it as the community's responsibility alone, but languages outside the Eighth Schedule of the Constitution need resources too.
sawal: How will the language travel from the school to the phone?
ref: Tenyidie
The language of the Angami community of Nagaland, which UNESCO has listed as a vulnerable language.
Ura Academy
A literary body in Kohima that works on preserving Tenyidie and Naga culture.

h: Adivasi lives dissolving in stone dust
dek: In the ramming mass factories of East Singhbhum, two or three years of dust is enough to finish off the lungs, and the cause of death is often written down as tuberculosis.
body: Msang Tudu had to work only three years in a ramming mass factory. Msang, thirty-nine, lives in Tetabadia village of East Singhbhum and says he does not have much time left. His wife Salge Tudu also died of the same disease after working a year in the same factory. Msang says he used to carry heavy sacks of silica powder.

Silicosis is caused by fine silica dust, which settles in the lungs and narrows the breathing tubes. Samit Kumar Kair, an activist of the Jharkhand group OSHAJ, says that in places like ramming mass units even less than two years of work is enough, and the belief that the disease comes only after ten years is wrong. Shrimat Soren, who breaks quartzite, says the daily wage was two hundred rupees.

Work here is mostly informal. Workers say they are not given safety equipment, and men cover their faces with a gamchha, a thin cotton cloth, and women with a sari. The Mines Act of 1952 and the Factories Act of 1948 lay down limits and compensation, but without a record of employment these rights stay on paper. According to the report, government doctors often write such cases down as tuberculosis, so that the responsibility for compensation does not fall on the state.

In villages like Gurabandha in East Singhbhum, hills full of quartzite have been cut and scattered over the last decade. After the National Human Rights Commission intervened in 2014, seventy-eight workers were identified in Jharkhand, but delay in inquiry and treatment continues. On 7 May 2026 the Jharkhand High Court said that uncontrolled mining and violation of the MMDRA law is a violation of the fundamental right to life.
nazar: This illness is not an accident, it is part of the system of production. The breath that is crushed in the dust of the industry that makes steel hides in the state's figures as tuberculosis.

The condition for compensation is a record of employment, and not having a record is the contractor's biggest defence. Until identity and treatment are tied to official papers, even the deaths will not be counted.
sawal: Steel made by selling lungs, whose account does it go into?
ref: Ramming mass
A powder used in the steel industry, made by grinding quartzite stone.
Silicosis
An incurable disease in which lung tissue hardens because of fine silica dust.

h: Samosa prices up, and the village prepares to be uprooted
dek: For Arvind Kurmi Patel, who sells samosas in Sarsela Rait in Damoh, costly gas and the tiger reserve's displacement plan have become the same question.
body: In Sarsela Rait of Damoh district, Arvind Kurmi Patel, who sells samosas, answered the rise in gas prices in his own way. He raised the price of one samosa from seven and a half to ten rupees and made each samosa a little bigger too. His plan was that the thirty per cent rise in cost would be covered by one extra spoon of filling, and that customers would stay with him.

The price of a fifteen kilo cylinder has gone from seven hundred fifty to nine hundred fifty rupees, and he needs two cylinders a week, because the oil has to stay hot continuously for frying samosas. Cylinders had become hard to get on time, so he asked his neighbours for help. In this village of more than three hundred people, half are Gond Adivasis, and Arvind has been selling samosas on the main road for ten years.

Monday is market day and on that day sales double. On ordinary days about a hundred samosas are sold, and on Monday double that, when urad dal pakoras are also added to the menu. Kneading the dough, boiling the potatoes and fetching water are done by his mother and his wife. Hot samosas are served on an old newspaper page, and Arvind makes the masala himself.

This same village is to be vacated, because it is among the ninety-three settlements of Virangana Durgavati, the country's fifty-fourth tiger reserve being set up in Damoh. Every adult is to get help of fifteen lakh rupees, but there is no clear word on compensation for the three acres of land that Arvind and his two brothers have. According to him, this package benefits only those who have no land.
nazar: In the counting of displacement, land shows up, the market and the customers do not. For those whose livelihood runs off the village road, setting up a shop in a new place is starting from the beginning.
The decision to conserve may be necessary, but its account should be demanded from the very person who was born there and earns there.
sawal: Why should a village shopkeeper bear the cost of saving the forest?
ref: Virangana Durgavati Tiger Reserve
A new tiger reserve of Madhya Pradesh being set up in Damoh, for which ninety-three hamlets are to be moved out.
Rehabilitation package
The help of fifteen lakh rupees to be given to every adult who moves out of the tiger reserve.

h: Siddi: still strangers after five hundred years
dek: Through the story of an eighteen-year-old runner and her mother, the DW documentary brings forward a community of African origin that India still does not recognise.
body: The film opens with a race. Eighteen-year-old Nimiksha Siddi runs towards the finish line, and the film's description calls her India's sprinting hope for the 2028 Olympics. Right here the film stops and opens a bigger question: very few people in India know about the community she comes from.

Nimiksha is Siddi. The ancestors of the Siddi community were brought to India from Africa five hundred years ago, as slaves or as hired soldiers. There is no exact figure for their population, which means even the state does not know properly how many they are. Many Siddis keep Siddi itself as their surname. They are among Muslims, Christians and Hindus, all three faiths. Many Indians take them for foreigners, and that is the sharpest part of the identity question.

The film's description says most Siddis live in poverty and make a living from daily wage labour or by collecting plants, honey and rubber from the forests. This community, tied to farming and forest work, lives in areas where government schemes reach the least, and where caste and race together close the roads to livelihood.

The film also recalls an old attempt. In 1983 the then sports minister started a plan to make Siddis into sprinters. Kamla Siddi was picked from the villages; she was thirteen then. She won several medals at the international level, including bronze and gold, could not fulfil the dream of training for the Olympics in America, but got a permanent job in the railways and a bigger house for the family.

Now the same family is coming into the country's eye through sport again, this time in the form of a daughter. The experiences of two generations, mother and daughter, move together. One generation changed its home by running, with the second the Olympic dream is now being joined. In between stands the same question that is in the film's title, why the work of recognising a community is being done through its players.

According to the film's description, racism and exclusion are both present in the everyday life of Nimiksha and her community. Applause and medals do not erase the discrimination that has to be borne every day in a market, a school or a government office. Sport here is certainly a way out, but it is not the only way either.

The film puts its claims with reference to the film's official page and its description. No scene or dialogue has been added. But what is clear is this, that a community is fighting for its identity and its livelihood at the same time.
nazar: Siddis came here before India's independence, yet they are taken for strangers. This question places caste and race together, because the path of discrimination here passes through both.
Success in sport cannot take the place of livelihood and respect for the whole community. If there is no work on forest produce, daily wages and land rights, one medal cannot become the whole story.
sawal: When will the burden of identity become lighter?
ref: Siddi
People of African origin, brought to India five hundred years ago as slaves or as hired soldiers.
Pentathlon
Five events within a single sport, such as running, jumping and throwing the javelin and the shot put.

h: Writing is a gamble, and the writer is alone
dek: Uday Prakash placed creation as lived experience, uncertainty and the question of freedom from ideologies.
body: The eighth instalment of Arthat was titled 'The stove of creation', and the speaker was the poet and story writer Uday Prakash. The start was with a staging of his story Nailcutter. The room was full of students and for two and a half hours no one was willing to get up and leave. The report says that after the staging there was a light moisture at the corners of many eyes, but that was not only the effect of the story, it was the knock of a compassion that is disappearing in our time.

Uday Prakash said Nailcutter was not an imagined experiment, it grew out of experiences he had lived. Then he comes to Muktibodh's third moment. The first moment is the direct experience of life and memory, without which no serious writing is born. In the second the writer decides to shape the experience into a particular form or genre. In the third, abstract feelings become words and part of public consciousness.

He called the process of writing a kind of gamble. The writer does not know which unknown shore the work will take him to, or how many people will understand its core. In this very uncertainty lies Bhavabhuti's hope that somewhere in a corner of the world some sensitive reader will surely be found. To turn personal experience into other people's story is true art, and one has to pay the price for speaking the truth.

He described the politics of art and political art as different, and said that erasing the difference between the two makes literature lose its best possibility. The story behind Mohan Das was also told, a man who had to prove again and again that he was alive because paper is taken as the final truth. Creation in the end is utter loneliness, but in that very loneliness a global hope survives.
nazar: This is a report of a literary gathering, but the questions raised in it are the real quarrels of Hindi literature today, ideology's claim over writing and the price of speaking the truth.
He called returning an award spiritually difficult and said that only someone who has taken such a step can feel it. This honesty is what makes this conversation necessary in today's atmosphere.
sawal: Can a writer stay free of ideology?
ref: Third moment
In a literary diary of Muktibodh, the idea of the writing process in three stages, which moves from experience to public consciousness.
Nailcutter
Uday Prakash's well-known story, whose own lived experiences were narrated at this gathering.

h: The ring inside a woman, the museum of the house
dek: In Rajesh Kamal's eleven poems the woman is present not like a subject but like a movement.
body: In the eleven poems of Rajesh Kamal published in Sammukh, the woman is present not like a theme but like a movement. Historical, imagined and unnamed women come into them, but the poet does not claim to speak for them. The editorial note rightly says that he does not descend into the whirlpool of mansplaining. The feeling is direct, the words are few, and in this very sparing lies the strength of the poem.

In the first poem a voice from days gone by returns. The girl left behind in the hurry to become a wife begins to tell her stories again, and in her laughter the ring of a raw age comes back. But this magic melts like a dewdrop in the first sun. The poet also writes that he had forgotten all the usual words of comfort.

On the other side is public grief. The Palestinian painter Heba Zagout was killed in Israel's bombing along with her two small children. The poem is about the colours of her paintings, the pigeons and the mass graves, there where hospitals are for the wounded and not for women giving birth. The poem about Ursula says that every house is a museum and in every house lives an unwritten Ursula.

The last poems are about power inside the house. The order is that lamp which was kept inside the threshold so that the house would stay lit, until it filled its palms with the sun. Consensus is what was called cultured and tolerant outside, while if the names inside were made public, governments would fall. In the moonless night the woman never raises her voice, and in the end she puts all the latches on herself.
nazar: Writing a poem about a woman is easy, claiming to speak for her is not. Here the poet puts himself in the place of the accused, and that is what separates these poems from a speech.
When questions are raised about a woman's voice and about her being in public, such poems turn the reader back to his own habits.
sawal: Does the poet speak for the woman or with her?
ref: Mansplaining
The habit of explaining a woman's experience to her by claiming to know it better than she does.
Ursula
The woman in Marquez's novel One Hundred Years of Solitude, whose story often stays within the walls of the house.

h: After a prize, why does everyone add up their own account?
dek: Using Anne Carson's Nobel as an occasion, Mayank Jain Parichha makes a wry joke of literary swagger and the fashion in criticism.
body: The article begins with a confession. Mayank Jain Parichha writes that he has not read Anne Carson and does not know when he will. He has passed the age of pretending to read, now only the pretence of being a writer is left. Even so he is writing the article, because a writer or a journalist becomes superfluous in people's eyes without writing something.

After Carson got the Nobel, everyone in literary gatherings began to show off their acquaintance with her or their lack of it. The writer read a long piece by the classicist Emily Wilson, in which Carson was compared with Rupi Kaur and Margaret Atwood and was called showy. He reads this with a sense of guilt, because we are used to finding some fault in a famous writer and then thinking better of ourselves.

The Hindi writer sitting inside the article, whom he calls his fooba, is happy that the Nobel also goes to light writers. Then comes the fear that tomorrow his own stories will be called childish. Questions rise like comedy. Is writing simply being light, is making a reel being light, will a seventy kilo writer also be counted as light.

In the end the talk comes to the essay. Carson wrote essays and still writes them, but who reads essays in Hindi. The writer says that in the age of AI the essay has become a dying form, then catches himself that only a paragraph ago he had said that essays are flourishing on Substack. This contradiction is not hidden, and that is the fun of this article.
nazar: After the Nobel announcement only two kinds of reactions come in Hindi, either a big claim or a big refutation. This article shows a third path, to write while accepting one's light standing.
This market of literary prestige runs not only in English, but in Hindi social media in the same way.
sawal: Is writing lightly a weakness or courage?
ref: Fox and Hedgehog
An idea from Isaiah Berlin's essay, in which the hedgehog knows one big thing and the fox many small things.
Fooba (uncle)
Here a joking name for that insider critic sitting in the Hindi literary circle, who doubts every big name.

h: Nineteen years later, the friend who paid the fees
dek: Vijayshree Tanveer's memoir writes of the shame of language, the tightness at home and a debt of friendship paid without telling.
body: The piece begins with that half month of the new year when people add up the last year's account and go slack. Nothing new has happened, only the calendar has changed, and the same old ache, the same boredom, the same fears remain. In this sameness the writer is saved by a wavering certainty that fate loves her.

In a journalism class the teacher is teaching the tricks of taking an interview fluently in English. The writer feels as if she is suffocating in English; she knows she can do better in Hindi, but stays quiet. Just then a girl raises her hand without any swagger and says that she is Hindi-speaking. Between the two, without a word, a kinship forms. She sings, she laughs openly, and her laughter keeps ringing in the ears like small bells.

The pressure at home is different. When asked for, the fee money disappears from the small purse and the father shouts that it would be good if you too were lost. The writer says she will drop the course. Her friend puts the fee receipt in her palm and says do not be sentimental. After that begins that seventeen-year-old forgetting in which addresses and phone numbers change.

The writer keeps searching for her on social sites like a mad person, but both names and faces have changed. In December, a notice about an e-card brings an old friend's photograph and number, and after nineteen years the two are together for an evening. This memory piece is about the shame of language, the tightness at home and that debt which her friend paid without telling her.
nazar: This memoir is a witness of a time when Hindi-speaking students in institutions teaching in English felt shame about their language and did not let it show.
Its biggest thing is that it holds a woman's friendship with the same dignity that love stories are given, without drama.
sawal: Who unloads the shame of language, and before whom?
ref: Memoir
A form that reads past times and people through the writer's present understanding, in which the experience is as much one's own as it is heard.
Raagdarpan
The first part of the title, which calls this writing a mirror that listens to the melodies inside.

h: The army cantonment and a Bhoti girl's silence
dek: Dharmchandra Prashant's Dogri story is set in Gilgit of 1940, where the difference between protection and possession keeps vanishing.
body: This Dogri story by Dharmchandra Prashant is set in Gilgit-Baltistan of undivided India, around the forties. Lieutenant Gyan has been transferred to Bunji, and even after three days he has found no place to walk. The Attock river flows with a swagger, and in front are the snow-laden peaks of Nanga, which the clouds keep hidden.

Gyan stops on seeing a girl sitting on a rocky mound, watching the waves. For soldiers, seeing a woman in the cantonment is like meeting God; he has lived two years in Gilgit and six months in Chilas and saw no woman there. As soon as the clouds clear, the girl folds both hands and bows to the peak of Nanga. Gyan asks in Bhoti where she lives, and she runs away.

The next day the girl is frightened, starts to run at the sound of stones, and when he tries to hold her hand, saying leave it, she disappears into the apricot orchard. Her name is Chainchalo, and she works in the mess because her mother is on the cot and her father has gone to Yarkand. Her mother folds her hands and says that they are very poor and do not let even the shadow of the soldiers fall on them.

Gyan promises that no one can say anything to Chainchalo. In the cantonment this closeness becomes talk, and the colonel warns that youth is a very bad thing. One dark night, returning from the orchard, someone pulls her hard and she falls, letting go of Gyan's hand. Gyan fires two or three shots from his revolver, she clings to him in fear, and he assures her that no one will come to know of this.
nazar: This story comes from a language that the mainstream of literature kept out for a long time, and its very presence today is an argument.
This relation between cantonment and village is the same even today, where the one claiming to protect sits at the top in the language of force and suspicion.
sawal: When does protecting another turn into a right over that person?
ref: Dogri
The language of the Jammu region, and Dharmchandra Prashant is held to have played a big role in bringing it to the literary mainstream.
Bunji
A small town on the bank of the Attock river near Gilgit, where there was an army cantonment in that period.

h: The 1898 book that fought men's superiority
dek: Maulana Mumtaz Ali's forgotten book turns the question of women into a debate about human rights.
body: Maulana Mumtaz Ali's book Huquq-ul-Niswan, published in 1898, is among the few books that did not keep the question of women limited to domestic reform or a debate on morality, but made it a question of human and social rights. On education, nikah, polygamy, divorce, inheritance, purdah and relations between women and men, this book argues with the prevailing notions of its time.

The central question of the first part is on what grounds, after all, man was taken to be better than woman, her ruler and the natural owner of her rights. Mumtaz Ali examines one by one the social, intellectual and religious bases of this claim. His argument is that man and woman are human beings of the same kind, and all the other differences rest only on being female and male.

In that period it was taken for granted that the man is the owner and women are subject to him, as if they were created only for his comfort. The difficulty is that this thinking is proved right not only out of bias, but in the name of justice, reason and God's will. That is why the aim of the book is to show the error of these ideas.

On the argument of physical strength, he asks how strength makes anyone a better human being than another; it only decides who gets the work that needs more effort. If strength were the test, then donkeys and strong animals would be above men. Referring to Razia Sultan and Nur Jahan, he shows that rule does not depend on being a man. On the argument of reason, he writes that when equal opportunities of health and education are not given, it is wrong to take men's lead as natural.
nazar: The arguments of this book written a hundred and twenty-eight years ago do not clash with today's feminist debate, they give it ground. Its biggest thing is that it tries to stop religion from becoming a weapon against women.
The loss of such books creates the illusion that the debate on women's rights came from outside. This article breaks that illusion.
sawal: Who turns a woman's subordination into a command of religion?
ref: Huquq-ul-Niswan
Maulana Mumtaz Ali's book on women's rights, published in 1898, whose first part is read in this article.
Nabuwwat
The office of prophethood, which has been used again and again as an argument to prove men's superiority.
